prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

The days are dog-eared, the edges torn, ragged—like those pages I ripped once out of library books, for their photos of Vallejo and bootless Robert Johnson. A fine needs paying now it’s true, but not by me. I am no more guilty than that thrush is who sits there stripping moss off the wet bark of a tree. A red fleck, like his, glows at the back of my head—a beauty mark, left by the brain’s after-jets. I would not wish for the three brains Robert required to double-clutch his guitar and chase those sounds he had to know led down and into a troubled dusky river, always. Three brains did Johnson no earthly good, neither his nor Vallejo’s 4 & 1/2 worked right exactly—O bunglers, O banged-up pans of disaster! Crying for days, said Cesar, & singing for months. How can I be so strong some times, at others weak? I wish to be free, but free to do what? To leave myself behind? To switch channels remotely? Better to sing. Not like the bird, but as they sang, Cesar & Robert— with the shocked & seeded sweetness of an apple split open by a meat cleaver.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: The, Vallejo, Robert

outputs.L1:
Here is a polished version that preserves the imagery, allusions, and fractured lyricism of the original while refining its cadence and diction:

---

The days are dog-eared now, their edges torn and ragged—like those pages I once tore from library books for their photographs of Vallejo, and of Robert Johnson, bootless. A fine is owed, it's true, but not by me. I am no guiltier than that thrush perched there, stripping moss from the wet bark of a tree. A fleck of red glows at the back of my skull, much like his—a beauty mark left by the brain's spent afterfire. I would not wish for the three brains Robert needed to double-clutch his guitar and chase those sounds he must have known led down, always, into some dusky and troubled river. Three brains did Johnson no earthly good, just as neither of Vallejo's four and a half worked quite right—oh, bunglers, oh, battered pans of disaster! Weeping for days, said César, and singing for months. How is it I can be so strong at times, and so weak at others? I want to be free—but free for what? To abandon myself? To flip through channels by remote? Better, then, to sing. Not as the bird sings, but as they sang, César and Robert—with the shocked, seed-strewn sweetness of an apple split open by a meat cleaver.
outputs.L2: Time has grown creased and worn at its corners, frayed at the margins—much like those library pages I once tore free, chasing images of Vallejo and a barefoot Robert Johnson. Someone owes a penalty now, that much is certain, though the debt isn't mine to settle. My innocence matches that of the thrush perched nearby, peeling damp moss from tree bark. A crimson speck, mirroring his, burns at the back of my skull—a birthmark left behind by my mind's own exhaust. I have no desire for the trio of brains Johnson needed to wrestle his guitar into submission, pursuing melodies he understood would only spiral downward into some murky, restless current. That triple mind brought Johnson nothing worthwhile, just as Vallejo's fractured intellect—four and a half brains, broken and misfiring—served him no better. What clumsy souls they were, what wrecked vessels of catastrophe! Cesar himself confessed to weeping for days on end, then singing through entire months afterward. Why does my strength ebb and flow so unpredictably? I long for liberation, yet liberation toward what purpose? To abandon my own identity? To flip through existence like changing stations? Singing seems the wiser path. Not the bird's simple tune, but the kind Cesar and Robert produced—carrying that startling, seed-scattered sweetness of an apple cracked open beneath a butcher's blade.
outputs.L3:
# On Tearing Pages and Owing Nothing

I remember pulling those pages loose—Vallejo's photograph, Robert Johnson's face staring out from the library binding, the paper giving way under my thumbnail with that small violence libraries are built to prevent. Somewhere there's a fine accruing, some ledger with my name half-attached to it, but I won't be the one to pay it. I feel about this the way a bird feels about the bark it strips for its nest: no crime committed, only necessity following its own logic, the body doing what the body does without consulting the register of guilt.

They say Robert Johnson had two brains, or three—that the crossroads gave him something extra, some second engine running under the hood of the ordinary skull. I don't want it. Whatever surplus he was given didn't save him; it walked him toward the poisoned bottle, toward the dark room, toward twenty-seven years and out. It didn't save Vallejo either, all his brilliance folding in on itself in a Paris hospital bed, asking what day it was, asking to be let go on a Thursday because Thursdays were when his misery had always been worst. Extra brains are not extra life. They are just more rooms for the trouble to move through.

Because that's what they both were, underneath the myth: bunglers. Banged-up pans of disaster, dented from the inside out. Genius doesn't arrive polished; it arrives the way Johnson arrived at that crossroads, if you believe the story—desperate, off-key, willing to trade anything for one clean run of notes. It arrives the way Vallejo arrived at his best poems, having already failed at so much else, having already buried friends and starved in rented rooms. These men cried for days. They sang for months. The suffering and the singing were not sequential—they were the same weather system, indistinguishable, one bleeding into the other until nobody, least of all the men themselves, could say where the wound ended and the music began.

So what is freedom, if not escape from all this? I used to think it meant getting out—out of the body, out of the history, out of the self that keeps waking up as itself every morning. But I don't think that's it anymore. I think freedom is not the absence of the self but the full presence of it, voiced. Freedom is not escaping into someone else's clean, unbothered life. It's staying exactly here, in the wreckage, and singing anyway.

Not the bird's song—not that effortless, weightless trilling that costs nothing because it risks nothing. I don't want that ease. I want the singing Cesar and Robert did: torn open, exposed, an apple split by a meat cleaver instead of peeled with a knife—the flesh still wet, the seeds visible, nothing hidden, nothing pretty about the cut but everything alive in it. That's the only singing worth doing. The kind that comes after the bark has already been stripped, after the fine is already owed, after the two brains have already led you somewhere you shouldn't have gone—and still, somehow, the mouth opens.
outputs.L4:
# What the Broken Ones Knew

I.

There is a guilt that lives in the hinge of the jaw,
that settles like sediment in the throat's slow river.
I have carried it through orchards gone feral,
past fences collapsed under their own rusted weight,
asking the crows what they know of forgiveness.
They know nothing. They only know black,
and the particular music of wings against cold.

II.

Vallejo said he would die in Paris on a day it was already raining
in his memory, and the rain came anyway,
grey and indifferent as a debt collector,
and he died as promised, a man who had written
his own ending into being, who understood
that the poem is sometimes a wound
we press against until it becomes a mouth.

What did it cost him, that seeing?
The stomach that never quite forgave the bread it ate.
The Andes folded into his ribs like a second, heavier heart.
Some men carry a whole country's grief
the way other men carry loose change—
absently, until it wears a hole clean through the pocket.

III.

And Johnson at the crossroads—
or not the crossroads, but something more mundane
and therefore more terrible: a room, a bottle,
a woman's husband with a reason.
The strychnine did not care about his gift.
It moved through him with the same blind patience
as anything moves through anything,
water finding the low places, fire finding air.

They say he tuned his guitar to something
just beneath the register of safety,
that when he sang, the notes arrived
already bruised, already knowing
they would not last the century unbroken.

IV.

I keep asking the wrong question.
Not: what did their suffering purchase?
Not: is the vision worth the rot that grew it?

The orchard does not ask why the frost came
before it teaches the fruit sweetness.
The frost simply comes. The fruit
simply learns to split rather than stay whole,
and what pours out surprises even the tree.

V.

Maybe freedom was never the door out of the self—
that door I keep pressing my whole body against,
expecting some hallway of pure light beyond it.

Maybe freedom is staying inside the wreckage
long enough to make it sing:
Vallejo's rain becoming psalm,
Johnson's hellhounds becoming hymn,
the guilt in my jaw becoming, finally,
a sound I am willing to make in daylight.

VI.

Somewhere a fruit falls and splits against a stone
not because it wanted to give up its sweetness
but because gravity does not negotiate,
and what spills out is shocking—
too bright, too much, entirely unearned
and entirely earned, both at once,
the way all real sweetness arrives:
by violence, by falling, by breaking open
exactly where we were too tender to hold.

Robert's story is one that reflects dedication and perseverance. Throughout his life, he demonstrated a commitment to the values that matter most: family, community, and hard work. Whether through professional endeavors, community involvement, or personal relationships, Robert Vallejo's influence extended beyond simple achievements. He understood that legacy isn't measured solely by accomplishments, but by the way one treats others and contributes to the fabric of daily life around them.

In remembering Robert Vallejo, we're reminded that every name carries a story, and every story—no matter how understated—deserves to be told and preserved.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem that weaves together Cesar Vallejo and bluesman Robert Johnson, using imagery of torn library book pages and birds.
counterfactuals.output:
**Crossroads Elegy for Two Ghosts**

Somewhere a library shelf is bleeding paper—
a page torn from *Trilce* flutters loose,
its Spanish half-eaten by damp,
*mañana* becoming *maña* becoming nothing,
and a blackbird carries the scrap in its beak
across a Mississippi field
where the corn stands like church pews
emptied of God.

Cesar, they say you knew the day you'd die,
a Thursday in Paris, rain
falling like a verdict,
and Robert, they say you knew the hour too—
some crossroads hour, dust and whiskey,
a man in a black coat tuning your guitar
to the pitch of the grave.

The bird doesn't care whose elegy it's stitching.
It flies with torn pages in its claws
the way it flies with twine, with hair,
with anything the world discards
to build a nest above the ruin.

*Me moriré en París con aguacero*—
you wrote it before it happened,
the way Robert hummed *hellhound on my trail*
before the dogs were even born,
before the poison in the glass
before the ink dried on the last verse
of a book someone would later
rip apart for kindling
or for wings.

Torn pages drift like sheet music no one plays.
Somewhere a crow reads Braille in the missing words,
somewhere a guitar string snaps
into the shape of a question mark,
and the birds—grackles, ravens, sparrows—
gather the syllables that fell
from both your mouths,
weave them into a single nest
built high in a tree that grows
between Lima and Clarksdale,
between the rain and the crossroads,
between the poem finished
and the song that never got to end.

I have stood beneath that tree.
I have watched the torn pages settle like snow
that refuses to be white,
and I have heard, in the hush after wingbeat,
your two voices merge—
one weeping in Spanish,
one moaning in a key
no hymnal owns—
singing the same low blues:
*I was here. I am leaving.
Look at what the birds
have made of what I left behind.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a confessional poem about guilt and creative suffering, referencing a poet and a musician who both died young and troubled.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Living Owe

I keep Plath's oven on my desk like a paperweight,
a joke I tell no one, though I mean it
the way you mean things after midnight—
half prayer, half provocation.

Thirty years old and still measuring my pain
against hers, against Cobain's feedback and silence,
that note he left too clean, too final,
the guitar still warm in some photograph.

I did not earn this inheritance.
I have never starved for a poem.
I have never opened a vein for a chorus
and called it Tuesday. But I've sat
with the blank page like it was a verdict,
have wanted the ache to mean something
larger than my own small weather.

This is the guilt: to want the wound
without the dying. To borrow the myth—
Sylvia's head in the oven, Kurt's shotgun
propped against the greenhouse—
and wear it like a coat I didn't buy,
didn't earn, will never have to return
because I'm still here, still breathing,
still writing this instead of living it.

They didn't choose the archetype.
They just wanted the pain to stop
and it did, permanently, while I sit here
turning their deaths into material,
another stanza, another line break
dressed up as reverence when really
it's theft—of grief, of gravity,
of every real thing they lost
so I could have a metaphor.

Forgive me, Sylvia. Forgive me, Kurt.
I am not comparing myself to you.
I am comparing myself to myself,
the poet I thought I'd have to become—
tortured, doomed, beautifully wrecked—
and finding instead just this:
a person with a laptop and coffee going cold,
still alive tomorrow, still alive
the day after that,
guilty of nothing
but survival,
which is its own kind of confession,
its own unbearable song.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal, lyrical poem comparing the speaker's inner turmoil to Robert Johnson's guitar playing and Vallejo's poetic anguish, ending on an image of an apple split by a cleaver.
counterfactuals.output:
# Crossroads Ledger

There is a string in me tuned to some other century's despair,
bent like Johnson's fingers on a Tuesday
that never learned to end—
his six strings six roads
all leading back to the same dry crossing,
the devil less a man than a debt
the body pays in tremolo.

I have swallowed my hunger the way Vallejo
swallowed Paris, that gray bread of exile,
his *César Vallejo ha muerto* already
a rehearsal, a wound he practiced
until it became prophecy, until Thursday
arrived wearing his name like a coat
too thin for the rain it was born to hold.

My turmoil does not announce itself.
It hides in the space between the beat
where Johnson's foot taps against nothing,
against the pine floor of some room
already halfway to myth—
and I understand this: to make of pain
an instrument, to make the instrument
outlive the hand.

Somewhere a train is always leaving
without me, its whistle the exact pitch
of Vallejo's loneliest comma,
the pause before *piedra* becomes *herida*,
before stone becomes wound
becomes stone again, the cycle
that asks nothing of forgiveness.

I carry these men in my sternum
like two tuning forks struck
against different griefs, and still
they hum the same low note—
the sound of something being split open
so what's inside can finally
be looked at, be counted, be named.

And here is the apple on the table,
red as a chord no one asked for,
and here is the cleaver, patient,
a single silver sentence—

and the sound it makes going through
is not violence. It is confession.
It is the seed's dark room
suddenly full of light,
two halves turned toward each other
like a man remembering
he once had a face,
like a guitar remembering
it was once a tree,

like grief, finally,
admitting it was only ever
trying to become fruit.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a poem in first person that mixes memories of stealing photographs from library books with meditations on genius, madness, and song.
counterfactuals.output:
# What I Took From the Stacks

I was seventeen and hungry for a kind
of theft that felt like scripture—
razor blade tucked in my coat sleeve,
waiting for the library to empty out
so I could kneel before the biography section
like it was an altar built for vandals.

Rilke's face, cut clean from page 34.
A photograph of Nina Simone
mid-scream, mid-song, her hands
raised like she was conducting weather.
I told myself I was preserving something,
not stealing it—that genius belonged
in a shoebox under my bed
more than in a book
nobody else would ever open.

I think now about the thin membrane
between brilliance and the thing
that eats brilliance alive.
How Schumann heard an angel dictate a theme
and woke up trying to drown himself in the Rhine.
How they say Van Gogh painted
with the same hand that later
couldn't stop shaking.
How song and sickness sometimes share
a single throat, a single fevered
instrument, and we call the noise
that comes out of it *genius*
only after the singer's dead enough
to be safely admired.

I have the photographs still.
Warped now, adhesive gone brittle,
the faces of the mad and the brilliant
(as if there's a difference)
curling at the edges like they're trying
to fold themselves back
into whatever book I tore them from.

I think about the librarian
who must have found the gutted pages,
the neat rectangular absence
where a face should be—
how she probably just sighed,
stamped something on an index card,
never knowing a boy had knelt there
trying to steal proof
that a person could break
so beautifully
it counted as music.

I didn't understand yet
that I wasn't stealing faces.
I was practicing a kind of hunger
I'd carry my whole life—
this need to hold a piece
of anyone who'd found a way
to turn their breaking
into something that could be sung.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a literary poem exploring the tension between weakness and strength, freedom and self-destruction, invoking Robert Johnson's crossroads myth and Cesar Vallejo's despair.
counterfactuals.output:
# At the Crossroads, Weeping

*for R.J. and C.V., who both went looking for God and found only the going*

**I.**
Midnight keeps no mercy in Mississippi,
only dust that remembers each footstep
as a debt. He knelt there — not to pray,
but because kneeling is what the body does
before it agrees to become an instrument.
Six strings, six wounds he'd carry north,
each one tuned to a hunger
too old to wear a name.

They say a tall man came
smelling of turned earth and unpaid rent,
took the guitar, handed it back
restrung with someone else's fingers.
This is how freedom sometimes arrives —
disguised as a favor,
its bill folded small enough
to forget until the throat closes.

**II.**
In Lima, another man was already dying
of simply being alive — Vallejo, who wrote
*hay golpes en la vida, tan fuertes… yo no sé*,
who weighed his mother's bread
against the bread the world allowed him
and found the scale obscene.
He never walked to a crossroads.
He was the crossroads —
Indian and Spaniard arguing in his blood
over whose god got to watch him suffer.

**III.**
Weakness is not the absence of strength.
It is strength grown tired of proving itself,
sitting down at last in the dirt
to let something larger use it.
Johnson bent his weakness into a moan
that outlived the whiskey that poisoned him.
Vallejo bent his into a comma
that never finds its sentence's end,
a wound that keeps its stitches loose
on purpose, so the light gets in
the way it gets into a grave
before the shovel's finished.

**IV.**
Both men knew the secret
freedom hides in its coat:
to be free is to be unheld,
and to be unheld
is to fall with style, if you're lucky,
into whatever waits below —
devil, or Paris rain,
a Thursday afternoon,
the collarbone aching
like a debt come due.

*I will die in Paris, in a downpour,
on a day I already remember* —
he wrote it before it happened,
the way Johnson must have hummed
his own dying in a minor key
years before the glass was poured.
This is what despair knows
that hope refuses to learn:
the crossroads isn't a place.
It's a tense — the future
perfect, the *having-already-lost*
that lets a man keep walking anyway,
guitar or pen
gone heavy in his hand,
because the road behind him
has already closed,
and the road ahead
was never truly open,
only bright enough to follow.

**V.**
So let the myth and the misery
shake hands in the small hours —
one signed in blood at a dirt crossing,
one signed in ink at a rain-dark café,
each of them praying the same prayer
in a different tongue:

*let me be ruined beautifully,
let my weakness sing,
let freedom cost exactly
what I am —
no more, no less —
and let that be enough.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
